common_name: Summer Sunset Asiatic Jasmine (Color-Changing Foliage Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Summer Sunset colors most vividly with several hours of direct sun each day but still performs well as a dense mat in fairly heavy shade, just with greener, less vivid foliage.

directions: Summer Sunset is a dwarf, color-changing sport of Asiatic jasmine grown for foliage that emerges bright apricot-orange and matures through mottled gold and gray-green, giving the low, twining mat far more seasonal color shift than plain green asiatic jasmine or even the white-splashed 'Snow N Summer'. Plant in well-drained soil and mulch between young plants until the dense, weed-suppressing carpet knits together; it shares the same tolerance for dry shade under trees and difficult slopes that makes the species so useful in Southern landscapes. Shear back hard every couple of years in early spring to remove old woody growth and refresh the most vivid new foliage color. Once established it is drought tolerant and needs little more than an annual tidy-up.

common_name: Tricolor Star Jasmine (Pink and Cream Variegated Confederate Jasmine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence; Tricolor shows its brightest pink and cream new growth in good light and fades toward solid green in deeper shade.

directions: Tricolor is a striking sport of confederate jasmine whose new leaves emerge soft pink and cream before maturing to dark green mottled with white, with foliage often flushing reddish in cool winter weather, giving year-round color beyond the species' glossy solid green. Train the twining stems onto a trellis, fence, or arbor, or let it sprawl as a slower-growing variegated groundcover; expect the same intensely fragrant, pinwheel-shaped white flowers as the straight species in warm-season flushes. It is slightly less vigorous and a touch less cold-hardy than plain confederate jasmine, so site it in a sheltered spot at the cooler edge of its range. Water regularly while young, then taper off once established, and prune after flowering to keep variegated growth dense and colorful.

common_name: Lemon Drop Carolina Jessamine (Dwarf Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter in full sun to shade; Lemon Drop's low, rounded, mounding habit needs no trellis and works well as a foundation planting, border, or large-scale groundcover.

directions: Marketed under the trade name Lemon Drop, this patented selection (cultivar 'Conrop') breaks completely from the twining, climbing habit of typical Carolina jessamine, instead forming a low, dense, rounded mound that never needs a support structure. Soft lemon-yellow, sweetly fragrant trumpet flowers cover the plant for four to six weeks beginning in early spring, with individual blooms lasting several days, and it is notably more cold-hardy than many jessamine cultivars, shrugging off winters into zone 6. It flowers most heavily in full sun but tolerates shade better than most Gelsemium selections, making it a useful compact choice for foundation plantings, slopes, or mixed borders rather than fences and arbors. As with all Gelsemium, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas where children or pets graze.
